doc.title: Fred Radke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Hillsdale, Michigan, November 8, 2023

title: How Harry James kept discipline, paychecks, malaria and playing the hits
summary: Harry's one-mistake rule, his hiring for attitude, his malaria, and a night when two trumpeters complained about the hits.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: His attitude. You know a trumpet player one night, a new trumpet player, and he missed an E on the end of “Shiny Stockings” [scats] and he cracked it, right? Because there’s no mistakes, no mistakes. Harry walked right back to the trumpet section. He says, “You know guys we play a physical instrument. I mean you know it’s a physical instrument, you know? And you know you’re allowed to make a mistake on my band once.” And he turned around and walked off.

See? See that’s it. Another thing that Harry James did, and I learned this from him too, he signed your paycheck. And sometimes, most times, he would hand you your paycheck. And I noticed this too when we were doing this a lot, when a guy says, “Thank you for the job” or just grabs it. Harry James would hire an individual that had a great attitude and maybe not the player that this guy is, but this guy has a lousy attitude, but this guy’s got a positive attitude. He’d keep the job. That’s what he wanted. And Harry would go through a stage, you wouldn’t know when to approach him and when not to approach him. Sometimes when he wasn’t feeling good, you know he had — one time we were on the road in Florida, his malaria flared up. He got malaria when he wintered in Texas with a circus band with his father’s band in Beaumont. I think that’s where he acquired it. And that’s why he never went in the service, he had those things. And one time he was really ill and he showed up at the gig and he didn’t — he hadn’t been drinking at all. And I caught that and Corky — I said, “Uh oh, now this is the serious Harry James.” And I don’t know these guys man, these two young trumpet players were standing there, the timing was awful, I never forgot this. These two guys says, “Man, you know something, we’re playing the same thing, ‘You Made Me Love You’ — ” Well Harry played all of his hit records, that’s what the people wanted him to do, and then we played what we wanted to do. See that’s the first thing you do. You play — Joe Graydon from Columbia Artists told me this. You have the Harry James Orchestra, you go out and you play every blockbuster. Bap bap bap. The people want to hear it. Then you can do what you want to do, do all the Thad Jones, Ernie Wilkins charts man, Neal Hefti charts, do whatever you want. But you’ve proven your point. What you’ve done with the audience is say you invited me in and now you’re confident that I’m in your front room now and now you’ve accepted me. Now I can do what the heck I want man. Okay? So here’s these guys there, saying “Why do we — ” And Harry’s standing there oiling his valves and he says, “Hi guys.” And I’m standing there with Corky and Corky says, “Look out.” So now we’re playing this thing and there’s ten thousand people in this arena or something, for a law
